groups.title: Redis Data Structures
groups.question: Explain how you choose the right Redis data structure and manage memory over time.

followUps.Strings, Hashes & Sorted Sets: Why is a Hash often better than a JSON string for storing a user session in Redis?
followUps.TTL, Expiration & Eviction Policies: What happens when cache keys never expire, and how do eviction policies change Redis behavior when memory runs out?

evidence.text: A JSON string must be read, parsed, changed and written back whole for every small update.
A hash stores fields separately, so one field can be read or changed directly.
Small hashes are also stored compactly.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (Hash, HSET) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a JSON string is always better than a hash.

evidence.text: Keys without a TTL never expire, so memory keeps growing.
A plain SET on refresh removes the old TTL.
At maxmemory, noeviction makes writes fail, and LRU policies remove keys (all keys or only those with a TTL).

notEnough: Only naming the terms (TTL, EXPIRE, maxmemory) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says Redis deletes old keys by itself without TTLs.

groups.title: Caching Patterns
groups.question: Walk through the main ways to keep a cache and a database in step.

followUps.Cache-Aside, Write-Through & Write-Behin: Compare cache-aside, write-through and write-behind, and name the main risk of each.
followUps.Cache Invalidation Strategies: What are the trade-offs between TTL expiry and deleting cache keys on every write?

evidence.text: Cache-aside reads the cache and fills it on a miss; risk: stale data and a stampede of misses.
Write-through writes cache and database together; risk: slower writes.
Write-behind writes the cache first and the database later; risk: losing writes if the cache fails.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (cache-aside, write-through, write-behind) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the three patterns behave the same.

evidence.text: TTL is simple but serves stale data until it expires.
Deleting keys on write is fresher, but every write path must know which keys to delete.
So it's a trade-off between staleness and complexity/coupling.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (invalidation, TTL) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says TTL expiry never serves stale data.

groups.title: Pub/Sub & Streams
groups.question: Explain how Redis can be used to pass messages between services.

followUps.Pub/Sub — Real-Time Messaging: What happens to a Pub/Sub message when no subscriber is connected, and when is that a problem?
followUps.Redis Streams — Durable Message Queues: In a consumer group, why must each consumer acknowledge messages, and what happens if it doesn't?

evidence.text: Pub/Sub only delivers to subscribers connected at that moment.
With no subscriber connected, the message is lost forever.
When messages must not be lost, use Streams or a real queue.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (Pub/Sub, PUBLISH) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says Pub/Sub stores messages until someone reads them.

evidence.text: In a consumer group each message goes to one consumer.
It stays in the pending list until that consumer acknowledges it (XACK).
Without acks the pending list grows and messages get re-delivered or stuck.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (Streams, XACK) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says messages are acknowledged automatically when read.

groups.title: Redis Persistence & Production
groups.question: Walk through what you need to think about when running Redis in production.

followUps.RDB Snapshots vs AOF Persistence: How do RDB snapshots and AOF differ in how much data you can lose after a crash?
followUps.Rate Limiting with Redis: Why is Redis a good place to keep rate-limit counters when you run many app servers?

evidence.text: RDB saves snapshots periodically, so a crash loses everything since the last snapshot.
AOF logs every write; with fsync every second you lose about a second at most.
AOF is more durable but bigger and slower; many setups use both.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (RDB, AOF) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

evidence.text: All app servers see the same counter in Redis, unlike in-process counters.
Atomic operations (INCR with expiry, or a Lua script) avoid races between servers.
Keys expire, so windows reset without cleanup.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (rate limiting, INCR) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says an in-memory counter in each server enforces a global limit.
